analysis.one_liner: Makes the Bush-era tax cuts, including lower rates on investment income, permanent.
analysis.headline: A bill to make the Bush-era tax cuts permanent drew 76 House Republican cosponsors but never received a committee vote or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cancel the expiration dates written into the 2001 and 2003 Bush tax laws, locking in permanently the lower income tax rates, the lower rates on dividends and capital gains, and the scheduled phase-out of the estate tax. It would also make permanent a federal deduction for state sales taxes, a deduction for college tuition, and a larger up-front write-off (expensing) that lets small businesses deduct new equipment immediately instead of over time. Nothing in the bill pays for these cuts, so every dollar of lost tax revenue adds to the deficit.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with high taxable incomes gain the most, because the bill locks in the top-rate cuts, the lower tax rates on dividends and capital gains, and the estate tax phase-down written into the 2001 and 2003 laws [S2][S3]. Middle-income families gain smaller amounts from extended rate cuts, the sales tax and tuition deductions, and the marriage penalty and child credit fixes that came with those laws [S2]. Small businesses gain from a permanent $125,000 immediate deduction for new equipment [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Extends the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts — including the lower rates on dividends and net capital gains and the estate tax changes — beyond their scheduled expiration in 2010, permanently [S2][S3].
Makes permanent the federal deduction for state and local sales taxes and for college tuition and related expenses, which were set to expire [S2][S3].
Makes permanent the $125,000 expensing allowance letting businesses deduct new depreciable equipment immediately, up from the baseline $25,000 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it became law, the federal government would collect less revenue permanently, and the difference would show up as larger deficits or as pressure to cut federal programs. The gains are concentrated at the top: the rate cuts on high incomes and the lower taxes on dividends and capital gains flow mainly to households with large paychecks and large investment portfolios, while families get smaller per-household amounts.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes the tax cuts permanent with no offsetting revenue, so the entire cost adds to the deficit [S3].

The provisions that cost the most — the top income rate cuts and the lower rates on dividends and capital gains — deliver most of their benefit to households with the highest incomes and the largest investment gains, which is why the bill is tilted toward concentrated wealth even though families also get some benefit [S2][S3].

Locking in the sales tax deduction helps taxpayers in the nine or so states that have no income tax while doing nothing for taxpayers in the rest of the country — an acknowledged geographic imbalance of this provision [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ordinary working families would see modestly lower federal income taxes, and small businesses would get a useful equipment write-off. But the largest and most permanent benefits go to the highest earners and to holders of stocks and other investments, and the bill includes no way to pay for any of it. An honest assessment: the middle-class pieces (tuition deduction, expensing) could have been continued on their own; attaching them to a permanent, unpaid-for extension of the top-rate and investment-rate cuts makes this primarily a bill for concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Randy Neugebauer of Texas introduced the bill on March 3, 2010, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day [S1][S5].
76 of the House's 178 Republicans signed on as cosponsors [S4].
The committee held no hearing, made no changes, and never voted the bill out; the House and Senate never voted on it, and it expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, the largest unpaid-for tax cuts for high earners and investment income were not locked in permanently. Federal revenue that the bill would have given up stayed available. Small business owners, middle-class families using the tuition and sales tax deductions, and investors continued to receive those benefits only as long as Congress kept extending them short-term, as it did at the end of 2010.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or a vote on the bill during the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 76 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and no vote ever took place [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill permanently extends the lower top income rates, the 15% tax rate on dividends and capital gains, and the estate tax phase-down from the 2001 and 2003 laws — provisions whose benefits flow overwhelmingly to the households with the largest paychecks and portfolios [S2][S3]. The cost is permanent federal revenue that otherwise funds programs and debt reduction.

industries.industry: Small business owners and equipment makers
industries.note: Permanent $125,000 immediate expensing for new equipment lets businesses deduct investments up front instead of over years, which is popular with small firms and boosts orders for equipment manufacturers [S2][S3].
The bill makes permanent the federal deductions for college tuition and for state and local sales taxes, which expire on their own [S2][S3].
